name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,371

entries.clue: Singer in Italian port to north-east (8)

blocks.note: Bari is the port on Italy's Adriatic heel, the harbour town setters reach for
the clue's own word, written out as it stands
the compass point in its map shorthand

annotation.surface: A singer who has turned up in an Italian port somewhere up towards the north-east.
annotation.walkthrough: A whole word of the clue is simply copied down rather than translated, which is easy to read past when the two chunks either side of it are doing proper work.
annotation.definitionFit: A baritone is the male voice between tenor and bass, so 'singer' names the man by the range he sings in.

indicatorNotes.cast: To cast is to throw, and thrown letters land in whatever order they happen to fall.

blocks.note: B is the standard single letter for British
anagram fodder, the five letters of India's first prime minister

annotation.surface: A British actor cast as Nehru in a film.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cast' sits perfectly in the surface as the people in a picture, which is why it takes a moment to hear it as an instruction. The enumeration rules out leaving the statesman's name intact.
annotation.definitionFit: Ben-Hur is the 1959 chariot-race epic, so 'film' points at the answer by naming the class it belongs to.

entries.clue: Wild sea god in coastal location (3,5)

indicatorNotes.Wild: Something wild is out of control, and letters out of control will not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters across three little words

annotation.surface: A wild sea god washing up somewhere along the coast.
annotation.walkthrough: The small word 'in' looks like the join between wordplay and definition and is fodder instead, which is why the letters never quite add up until it is counted.
annotation.definitionFit: San Diego sits on the southern California shore, its bay and beaches making 'coastal location' a fair pointer to the city.

blocks.note: the nautical sense: the rope or strut that holds a mast upright
the vote, not the rigging: remaining is what the word asks for

annotation.surface: Backing offered to somebody who wanted to remain.
annotation.walkthrough: A Remainer is a Briton who voted in the 2016 referendum to keep the country in the EU, so the second half turns on politics while the first is still talking about rigging.
annotation.definitionFit: A stay is the rope or strut that holds a mast upright, and what a Remainer wanted was for Britain to stay in the EU.

entries.clue: Dancing seen to involve whitish people (8)

indicatorNotes.Dancing: Dancers keep swapping places, so the letters move about instead of standing in line.
indicatorNotes.to involve: To involve something is to draw it right into what is going on, so the letters close round it.

blocks.note: the four letters reset into this order, so that a gap opens in the middle
a pale face is a whitish one, drained of colour

annotation.surface: A dance that draws some pale-looking onlookers into it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'People' wants a nation, not a crowd on the floor. Nepalese serves as both the adjective and the plural noun for that nation, which is why no S is needed at the end.
annotation.definitionFit: The Nepalese are the people of Nepal, the word standing as the collective noun for the nation as well as its adjective.

entries.clue: Kind of bishop to leave bin out (2,1,3)

indicatorNotes.to leave: To leave is to go from where you were, so the letter named walks out of the word that held it.

blocks.note: the bishop on a chessboard is written B, and this is the letter that goes
BIN with that B gone
someone out for the afternoon is away

annotation.surface: Telling a bishop to put the bin out.
annotation.walkthrough: The bishop is the chess piece rather than the clergyman the bin-day surface offers, and the definition is the hedging phrase you reach for when something is only partly true.
annotation.definitionFit: 'In a way' is the qualified yes — true up to a point — which is exactly the hedge that 'kind of' performs in speech.

indicatorNotes.touring: A tour goes all the way round its destination, so the letters doing it wrap around the next piece.

blocks.note: gen is British informal for information — give me the gen — and these three letters open up after the first
L is the clothing label's large

annotation.surface: A dope being shown round a large Scottish valley.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dope' has three senses on offer — the idiot, the drug and the information — and only the last one is any use. Glen is the Scots word behind Glencoe and every whisky label.
annotation.definitionFit: A glen is the Scots word for a narrow valley between hills, the kind Highland place names are full of.

blocks.note: a lame excuse is a weak one
the New Testament, twenty-seven books bound as one collection

annotation.surface: Deploring somebody's feeble shelf of books.
annotation.walkthrough: NT for the New Testament is a pair worth banking, since 'books' and 'collection' both point at it. 'Weak' is lame in the sense of feeble, nothing to do with limping.
annotation.definitionFit: To lament something is to voice grief or regret over it, which is what deploring a state of affairs comes to.

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a specimen of vocabulary, something you could look up and pronounce
the reading the setter means: not how long that word runs but what it is the word for, the whole run of characters English writes with

annotation.surface: Hunting for a word that runs to twenty-six letters.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Of' is doing all the work, since it can mean made out of or belonging to. Checking the enumeration against the surface kills the jaw-breaking-long-word reading straight away.
annotation.definitionFit: The alphabet is precisely the set of twenty-six letters English is written in, so the clue names it by its contents.

blocks.note: slang for thoroughly intoxicated, whether by drink or anything else
the plain adverb of position, what prices and spirits are when they rise

annotation.surface: Something wrecked beyond repair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Smashed up' reads as one phrase about wreckage and has to be torn in two before either half means anything. Four letters is not much room for a demolition.
annotation.definitionFit: Smashed and high are both slang for intoxicated, and something high is simply up — raised above where it started.

indicatorNotes.regularly: Something done regularly comes round at fixed intervals, so the letters are taken at every second step.

blocks.note: every second letter of BLUEJAY, counting from the second: b-L-u-E-j-A-y

annotation.surface: A bluejay that shows up in a meadow at regular intervals.
annotation.walkthrough: The count starts on the second letter, not the first, which is the choice to test whenever a regular-letters instruction appears. Lea is the poet's word for open grassland, as in the lowing herd winding o'er it.
annotation.definitionFit: A lea is a meadow or stretch of open grass, a word that survives mainly in poetry and in crosswords.

indicatorNotes.prepared: Food prepared has been chopped and stirred about, so the letters come out in an order of their own.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eight letters

annotation.surface: Roger getting a dip ready in good time for the party.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Time' is prison time: doing porridge is British slang for serving a sentence, fixed in the language by the 1970s sitcom of that name.
annotation.definitionFit: Porridge is British slang for a spell in prison, from the oatmeal that was the standard jail breakfast.

entries.clue: Bad omen misplaced about river dog (8)

indicatorNotes.misplaced: Something misplaced has ended up where it does not belong, so the letters take new positions.
indicatorNotes.about: One thing set about another has gone right round it, closing on both sides.

blocks.note: the seven letters reset into this order, so that a gap opens halfway
R is the setter's river, no particular one named

annotation.surface: A bad omen turning up in the wrong place, out by the river.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' has to be heard as an instruction rather than as a vague somewhere-near, and the river is the bare letter setters use instead of naming an Exe or an Ouse.
annotation.definitionFit: A Doberman is a breed of dog, the sleek black-and-tan guard dog, so 'dog' names the class the answer sits in.

entries.clue: Student group long to finish early (4)

indicatorNotes.to finish early: Finishing early means stopping before the end, so the last letter never gets written.

blocks.note: long is the verb here, wanting something badly, which these five letters spell
the N standing at the end is the letter left off

annotation.surface: A group of students longing to be let out early.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long' is the verb, not the adjective the surface wants, and the definition is the school sense of the word rather than the calendar one.
annotation.definitionFit: A year is the whole cohort of students who started together — the sixth year, the class of 2026 — not just a span of months.

blocks.note: A is the single letter for American
chaps is the everyday British word for men
an able seaman is a fit one, up to the work

annotation.surface: American chaps who are fit and willing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fit' means able rather than healthy or good-looking, and 'American' shrinks to its initial while 'chaps' stays a whole word — two very different treatments side by side.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone amenable goes along with what is asked, willing to be led or persuaded rather than digging their heels in.

entries.clue: Live with a rook: ferocious creature (4)

blocks.note: to live is to be
the clue's own article, taken as it stands
the rook is the castle in chess notation, R

annotation.surface: Sharing a house with a rook, which turns out to be a ferocious creature.
annotation.walkthrough: The rook is the chess castle rather than the black bird the surface puts in the garden, and 'live' is the verb be, not the adjective of live wires.
annotation.definitionFit: A bear is the heavy, dangerous animal of forest and tundra, so the definition points at it by reputation rather than by name.

entries.clue: Girl with pain in both sides (6)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something has that something standing on either side of it.

blocks.note: right and left are the two sides, R and L, with a space opening between them
a dull pain is an ache

annotation.surface: A girl with a pain down both sides of her.
annotation.walkthrough: R and L are right and left, and they have to be read as letters rather than as the directions the aching body of the surface suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: Rachel is a common girl's name, biblical in origin, and the clue asks for nothing more particular than that.

entries.clue: Bachelor back to welcome the rest (8)

indicatorNotes.to welcome: To welcome someone is to take them in, so the piece named goes inside the letters that greet it.

blocks.note: B is the degree and the single letter for bachelor
the back of anything is its rear, and these letters open up before the last one
the clue's own article, taken as it stands

annotation.surface: A bachelor turning back to welcome everybody else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The rest' looks like one phrase for the remainder, and it splits: only the last word is the definition, so the answer is a pause rather than what is left over.
annotation.definitionFit: A breather is the short pause for breath you take in the middle of hard work, which is simply a rest.

indicatorNotes.about: Set one thing about another and it goes right round it, closing on both sides.

blocks.note: too means also, and these three letters open up before the last
to bag a bargain or a seat is to seize it

annotation.surface: Being about to grab an island as well.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as one phrase meaning on the point of, and it has to come apart before either word will work. Tobago is the smaller partner in the Caribbean nation of Trinidad and Tobago.
annotation.definitionFit: Tobago is a Caribbean island, the smaller half of the two-island state of Trinidad and Tobago.

indicatorNotes.shortly: Shortly means cut short, so the name it follows gives up its final letter.

blocks.note: Alec Guinness, the actor of The Bridge on the River Kwai and the first Obi-Wan Kenobi
the C at the end is the letter dropped

annotation.surface: A quick drink with one of the Guinnesses.
annotation.walkthrough: The surname is the actor's, not the stout's, though the definition works hard to keep the brewery in mind. 'One' is how setters introduce a person about to be named.
annotation.definitionFit: Ale is beer, the everyday British word for the pint you order at the bar, so 'Drink' names it by its broadest class.

blocks.note: a deal wrapped up is settled, finished with
the cook's sense: the joint has had long enough and can come out

annotation.surface: A parcel of food wrapped and ready to eat.
annotation.walkthrough: The two halves run together into one picture of a packed lunch, which is what hides the join. Neither half is the literal wrapping the surface offers.
annotation.definitionFit: A job wrapped up is done, finished; and meat is done when it has cooked through and can be served.

blocks.note: to go, in the nursery sense of needing the lavatory, is to pee
R for Rex, the Latin king of coins and royal monograms

annotation.surface: A nobleman heading off in the company of the king.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To go' is the euphemism for the lavatory rather than for departing with royalty, which is the whole gag. Rex is the king on every British coin.
annotation.definitionFit: A peer is a member of the British nobility — duke, earl or baron — entitled to a seat in the House of Lords.

indicatorNotes.initially: Initially points at the start of a word, so only the letter it opens with is taken.
indicatorNotes.in: Something in a thing sits inside it, with the rest of the letters closing round.

blocks.note: a bat is a club, a shaped length of wood to swing, and these letters open after the first
the letter the word starts with

annotation.surface: A terror who was recognised at the club.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Club' is the wooden weapon rather than the nightspot the surface books a table at, and 'terror' is the affectionate word for a child rather than fear itself.
annotation.definitionFit: A brat is a badly behaved child, and calling such a child a little terror is the ordinary English for it.

entries.clue: Geniality from one in good French house (8)

indicatorNotes.in: What is in something has that something closing round it on both sides.

blocks.note: bon is the French for good
a house you live in is your home, and these letters open up before the last
the Roman numeral for one

annotation.surface: Good humour found in a French household.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Good French' asks for the French word rather than for a good Frenchman. The answer is itself a French import, from bonhomme, a good-natured fellow.
annotation.definitionFit: Bonhomie is cheerful good nature, the easy friendliness of a host among guests, which is what geniality names.

entries.clue: Tentacle finally flung out in swamp (6)

indicatorNotes.finally: Finally points at the end of a word, so only the letter it closes with is taken.
indicatorNotes.out: To be flung out is to be out of place, and letters out of place settle into a fresh arrangement.

blocks.note: the letter the word ends with
anagram fodder, five letters

annotation.surface: The end of a tentacle flung out into a swamp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Swamp' is the verb to flood, not the marsh the tentacle conjures up; read as a noun it sends you hunting for bog country that will never fit six letters.
annotation.definitionFit: To engulf something is to swallow it up completely, as a wave swamps whatever it breaks over.

indicatorNotes.occupies: To occupy a place is to sit inside it, so the letter named settles within the others.

blocks.note: re means on the subject of, as in a memo headed re your letter
a liner is the ocean-going passenger ship
Charlie is C in the NATO spelling alphabet

annotation.surface: The chair Charlie sits in aboard ship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'On' is the setter's re, the word at the head of a memo, and it has to stop meaning aboard before the deckchair picture will let go.
annotation.definitionFit: A recliner is the padded armchair whose back tips and footrest rises, so 'chair' names it by the plain class it belongs to.
